Pour this mixture on top of the pumpkin, and then bake it off in a 375° oven for around an hour, or until the pumpkin is very soft.  It should start to look like pie crust; if it hasn't started to look like pie crust, add a little bit of water to the pan before the final bake. Finally, don’t worry too much about it actually being completely pumpkin pie.  There will be chunks of pumpkin mixed in, along with cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, and all the other spices, and also a bit of salt and sugar.  To assemble the pumpkin pie, top it all off with whipped cream (it even goes well with ice cream, if you care to serve it warm!), sprinkle with more powdered sugar, and enjoy!

prompt: Human: What can you tell me about the philosophy of John Locke
response:
Of all the philosophers who have influenced Western thought, John Locke may be the most influential for those who are thinking about pursuing a career in politics or law.  In particular, his views on government have been particularly influential in both political science and American law and politics.   If you’re just interested in philosophy as a whole, here are some of the core ideas about Locke you should try to understand:

Locke was a strong believer in the legitimacy of governments based almost entirely on their ability to protect citizens from harm.  While he did not actually believe this was possible, he believed people would come to believe it for themselves if governments did what they should do to keep them safe. 

Locke had a particular distrust of religious concepts that might allow bad rulers to manipulate people by convincing them the “God” they believed in was keeping an eye on them.  As the political theorist John Rawls has noted, Locke believed people would believe whatever rulers told them they were doing for their own good, whether it was really true or whether it could be proven false. 

Locke believed there should be no restrictions on people’s freedom of speech, thought or religion.  To him, all this should be able to lead to a more efficient, happier society and help people to enjoy their lives more.

Locke believed that people should have the opportunity to own property and make their own money.  But people should not own more than they could reasonably afford to keep themselves and their families alive. 

His view of what constitutes a “right” was very different than modern day American and Western philosophy.   In particular, he believed rights came not from the consent of the people, but rather from something within humans that makes them good citizens of a nation.   There is no concept of “constitutional” rights in Locke’s philosophy (as there is in the U.S.) and he did not think of the government as having the power to make any rules they wanted.

Locke was interested in the idea of “taboos”.  For example, in a free society we should not be shocked by seeing a parent abusing their child, or cheating on a spouse, or smoking, drinking and/or using drugs or committing suicide.   This sort of thing is considered acceptable practice in societies that value freedom.   In contrast, in a totalitarian society you can expect to face punishment unless you break some laws, and might even see the death penalty as acceptable if a government believed they deserved it.   Locke saw this sort of situation as one of its biggest problems and tried to fight against it in his philosophy by insisting on rights that people could not just break by simply refusing to obey rules about them.  

He also believed that there should be a separation of the church and state, but he didn’t want to put a wall between people and their God.   If there were no laws that said people had to believe in the God that the rulers used to be appointed by, they might still do what they believed was right in their hearts, and that could be very problematic for rulers and society as a whole.   But Locke’s belief in “taboos” also meant there was no real harm in using religion to justify what people did (for example, if a ruler said a death sentence in some cases was justified because the death penalty made the defendant’s life better).  This didn’t mean Locke believed this was right, but he did believe it was OK.  

Locke had a strong dislike of people not having the chance to defend themselves against others that might do them harm.  This included not having the knowledge to protect yourself in case of an accident, or not having an understanding of how to keep safe from physical harm or sexual assault.  

Locke was not very concerned with issues of women or minorities.   He had no particular problem with women’s emancipation and wanted to see that they should not be expected to be subservient to men, but rather that they should have equal rights to men.   He also believed people shouldn’t have to work to pay taxes if they wanted to avoid it and felt the concept of work itself was important to civilization.  If people were truly happy, they didn’t need to go to work, and some of the poorest people in history were not very unhappy.

As far as science goes, Locke believed that ideas should be accepted or rejected by the community as a whole, not just by experts or those people who had the same ideas as an expert.  This was a problem in that there were scientific communities that would do things for scientific reasons that weren’t in the common interest of society as a whole.  One example of this was when germ theory was developed, people would work very hard to show how harmful the bacteria were, even when it might hurt their professional reputation.   In contrast, Locke believed that ideas should be judged by their worth as a whole to the society it was being made for, based on whether it had the potential to help people, even if it hurt scientists personally.

prompt: Human: When were smart phones first made?
response:
Smart phones, as we currently know them, were first developed in the late 1990s by a group of engineers at Bell Labs in the United States. They were initially called “大哥大”, named after their size, but eventually their nickname stuck. 

In November 1993, AT&T and Lucent decided to compete with the Japanese mobile operators by developing a new type of cell phone. The idea was to put two small antennas on each piece of equipment and use a shared network to send text messages and fax messages.

As with many innovations from the 1990s, the first mobile phones ran on an OS called CP/M (Computing Systems Man-made, Inc.), which was later adopted as the first version of Windows by Microsoft. Bell Labs’ first prototype smartphone ran Linux, but it wasn’t until the second generation device that Windows found its way into it.

The idea was simple: the user would operate a phone by pushing buttons on the device. They would then communicate through a shared Wi-Fi network called CDMA, which is the type of technology used on most smart phones in the world today. Bell Labs’ prototype also used Bluetooth technology to transmit data between phones.

Bell Labs’ prototype was developed with software written by Peter Thimmesh, a researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. Their work, which formed the basis of AT&T’s initial concept for a cell phone, was published in the August 1994 version of IEEE Communications Magazine.

AT&T received support from a number of companies for their mobile phone project and was able to obtain funding from Intel and the Department of Defense. In March 1995, AT&T partnered with Lucent to form the U.S. Cellnet Corporation. The two were able to secure the intellectual property associated with their work and the pair filed for patents in connection with the U.S. Cellnet’s development in September 1995 and October 1996.

AT&T became a competitor in the market when the first generation of smartphones were released in November 1996, with a major push by the company starting in the fourth quarter of 1997.

The first smartphones to hit the market were LG CD-200 and Samsung C100. IBM also released their IBM MobileFirst platform and BlackBerry released their BlackBerry Sync software and Bluetooth technology. 

By the summer of 1998, AT&T and Lucent signed contracts to manufacture mobile phones in two states: New York and Illinois, for a total of up to 15 manufacturing sites in each state. The first phone that was intended for commercial production was the C100, but many others were also on the way.

The C100 was initially released in the US in December 1996, followed by the C200 in April 1997. AT&T sold their original 5 million devices in the first half of 1998. They are credited with launching the personal mobile phone as we know it today. prompt: Human: I have to help plan a wedding and I have no experience with it. What are some things I need to know about wedding planning?
response:
Here’s what I know.  First off, a wedding is a big deal, and there’s a lot for you to do.  It’s a culmination of a long series of events, from the engagement to the bachelor and bachelorette parties.  You’ll often be assigned to work on one of these components, and you may find other people you work with to be equally involved, especially if you’re involved with logistics.  Wedding planning can be divided into many small components, which give it a much larger picture perspective.  This means a little planning can go a long way in saving time and stress later.  A great place to start is with your venue.  Most weddings will be held in a location that can be rented out by groups of people, such as a banquet hall, hotel or even an event space in a private residence, such as a barn or a cottage.  Other venues that are often selected for weddings include restaurants, performance venues, wedding chapels and parks.

Another aspect of wedding planning to consider is your budget.  Wedding planning is a big business, with vendors and planners charging according to a sliding scale, so be sure to find a person or company that works within your means.  It is important to also be careful about overspending, as your budget will largely depend on your personal financial status.

One more thing to think about is how many people you want to be involved, for obvious logistical reasons.  A wedding event will typically have at least the officiant, the bride/groom, their parents/cohabitants, any wedding party members, the photographer/video crew and themselves.  

What comes next is really the work involved in throwing the wedding.  This typically involves hiring the ceremony planner or officiant, the caterer, the bartender, the bartender, the wedding dress and tuxedo shop, the florist, the band and/or DJ, and the wedding planner.  If the couple likes to handle these details themselves, these should be candidates for being included in the budget as well.  
Once these services and supplies are hired, the couple should set out to research and select vendors and/or locations for all other supplies and services: the cake baker, the hair and makeup salon, the limo service, etc.  Most vendors will have a list of recommended services that they can recommend, which would be a good starting point when selecting a vendor.  
To ensure that each aspect is handled professionally, it can be helpful to create a checklist and timeline, and try to work as closely as possible with each vendor you choose.  

When all these details are finalized, the couple, the wedding party, the officiant and any other guests can be organized into their respective seating arrangements, and the couple can start choosing their wedding attire.  
Next up will be deciding where to get the rings, and planning on the way the wedding cake will be served.  Then the rehearsal will happen, and the bride and groom will probably try on their wedding outfits, giving feedback to the person helping with the final arrangements, whether it’s the wedding planner or a trusted friend.  The ceremony will take place, the first dance is usually chosen by the couple, and then the reception starts.  

I hope that this information is helpful as you start the job of planning a wedding!

(BTW, this site originally had a “How to Plan a Wedding” page, but it doesn’t exist anymore.  If you or someone you know needs help planning a wedding, please ask, we’d be happy to help!)
